title: The king and the meal
hookLine: Narada knew every Veda and was still hungry; the sutras answer with a king and a meal
carry: bhakti is lived, not just known

cards: Year two met Narada in the Chandogya Upanishad, sitting before the sage Sanatkumara with a whole library in his head: all four Vedas, the old stories, grammar, mathematics, the stars. Then he said the honest sentence.
Sir, I know the sacred texts, but I do not know the Self. And I am in sorrow. Take me across.
Hold on to that scene, because today the Narada Bhakti Sutras ask the same question about love. If love is above the other roads, how do you get it? Isn't knowledge the way in?

teach.h: SOME SAY: KNOWLEDGE IS THE MEANS.
teach.b: The sutras answer the way they did on the marks of love in year two: they let several voices speak.
Some say, the text reports, that knowledge alone is the means to bhakti: you have to know who the Lord is before you can love him.
Others say knowledge and love depend on each other: picture two cards propped into a little tent.

teach.h: THE SONS OF BRAHMA: ITS OWN FRUIT.
teach.b: Then a third voice, the sons of Brahma, whom commentators take to be Sanatkumara and his brothers, the ever-young sages of the Puranas. Sanatkumara: the same teacher who heard Narada admit his learning hadn't freed him.
They say bhakti is its own fruit, not produced by something else.
Here the sutras side with them, and give their evidence: a king, a house, and a meal. Knowing about a king doesn't make the king pleased with you. Knowing about a meal doesn't end your hunger.
So, the sutras conclude, those who long for freedom should take up love itself. Notice what they don't say. Not that knowledge is bad, or that you should stop learning.
Narada was a great scholar. The sutras just refuse to let knowing about stand in for the thing. That's why devotional Hindus don't stop at reading.
They sing the names, offer the lamp, stand for darshan, take prasad.
The scripture tells you about the meal; worship is where you eat. The king has to be met. The meal has to be eaten.

how: Teachers of the Narada Bhakti Sutras use the king and the meal to explain that devotion is something lived, not only studied, and pair the study of the text with worship, singing and service.

o: a reward given to those who study hard
love that is its own fruit, not made by knowing
knowledge of God learned from the scriptures

games.q: the king and the meal — tap the pairs.
p: knowledge and love lean on each other

s: the sutras tell people to stop learning
they don't say knowledge is bad. they only refuse to let knowing about stand in for love itself.
the sutras side with those who say love is its own fruit
they agree with the sons of Brahma, and give the king, the house and the meal as evidence.
the sutras give only one view on the means to love
they report several: knowledge, each leaning on the other, and love as its own fruit.

games.q: three views on how love is reached are set before you. which one do the sutras themselves side with?
o: knowledge and love depend on each other.
games.why: they side with the sons of Brahma: love is its own fruit. knowing about a king doesn't please him, and knowing about a meal doesn't end hunger.

practice: Bring to mind someone or something you love and notice, for a few breaths, how much you know about them: their habits, their history, the facts.

Then let the facts go quiet and simply be near them, the way you'd sit beside someone without needing to talk. If you pray, you can do this with God, setting aside what you know about God for a while.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. For the sutras, its own fruit: knowing about the king doesn't please him, and knowing about the meal doesn't feed you.

orig.note: Sanskrit phala, fruit: the sutras call bhakti svayam phala-rūpā, of the form of its own fruit.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakti is lived, not just known. Knowing about the meal isn't eating it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 28–33 (knowledge as means; mutual dependence; the sons of Brahma: its own fruit; the king, the house, the meal; so take up bhakti)
